top row: what the decoder has so far, starting from <s>; bottom row: the German it has written
Decoder step 1 of 6: writing Das, reading mostly The
Decoder step 2 of 6: writing Gesetz, reading mostly law
Decoder step 3 of 6: writing wird, reading mostly will
Decoder step 4 of 6: writing nie, reading mostly never
Decoder step 5 of 6: writing perfekt, reading mostly perfect
Decoder step 6 of 6: writing sein, reading mostly be
Done: six steps for six German words, one encoder pass
Encoder: one step for all six English words
Illustrative: the German words and attention strengths are not from the paper. One layer and one of eight heads shown;
the model stacks six encoder and six decoder layers and decodes with beam search over 4 candidates, not one greedy word.
WHAT HAPPENS, IN ORDER

a.data-tip: Keys, values and queries all come from the previous encoder layer, so each position attends to all positions of the layer below. The encoder maps the sentence to one vector per word; given those, the decoder then generates the output one word at a time.
a.text: Every English word looks at every
English word, all six at once. Out

a.data-tip: Each decoder position attends to all decoder positions up to and including itself. In training a mask sets the scores of later positions to minus infinity; when generating, later words do not exist yet.
a.text: at the German written so far, itself

a.data-tip: Queries come from the previous decoder layer; keys and values come from the output of the encoder, so every decoder position can attend over all positions of the English sentence.
a.text: output for what to translate next.
Thick line: the English word it
reads most, into the word written.

a.data-tip: The model is auto-regressive: at each step it consumes the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. The paper decodes with beam search of size 4 rather than one greedy word.
a.text: It writes one German word, which
is fed back in as the next input.
Repeat until the sentence is done.
